title: Beef tallow & rose bar soap
subtitle: A hard, creamy bar with a traditional rose scent
excerpt: Cold-process bar soap made on rendered beef tallow with a small addition of sweet almond oil, scented with rose fragrance oil. Tallow gives one of the firmest, longest-lasting bars in cold-process making, with a conditioning lather. Yields eight bars; hardens in 4-6 weeks.
sourceNotes: Anne Bramson, Soap: Making It, Enjoying It (1972), tallow-based traditional recipes and SAP values. Susan Miller Cavitch, The Soapmaker's Companion (1997), tallow soap characteristics, cure guidance. Soap-Calc SAP table (accessed 2026): beef tallow 0.141, sweet almond oil 0.136. USDA AAS oil-FA data for tallow composition. Rose fragrance oil usage rate: 3% of oil weight; confirm your supplier's flash point before use.

recipe.batchNotes: Recalculate lye if you change the fat blend. Tallow SAP is 0.141; note this differs from lard (0.138). Rose fragrance oil should be added at light trace, not blended.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Tallow bars harden and improve for up to a year. Make a batch several months ahead if possible.
recipe.shelfLifeNotes: 2 years in a cool, dry place. The rose fragrance fades over the first year; the bar keeps its quality longer. Discard at any sign of DOS (orange spots) or rancid smell.

glossaryTerms.definition: The reaction between fat (here, beef tallow) and sodium hydroxide that produces soap and glycerol. Tallow has a higher SAP value than most vegetable oils, so the lye calculation differs from olive- or coconut-based recipes.
The percentage of fat left unsaponified in the finished bar. A 5% superfat on a tallow bar leaves conditioning fatty acids in the bar.
The point at which the blended soap batter holds a faint drizzled trail on its surface, the signal to add fragrance and mould.

content.text: Beef tallow and rose soap is a firm, creamy-lathering cold-process bar built on rendered beef fat. Tallow produces one of the hardest, longest-lasting bars in home soap-making, with a clean conditioning lather that rinses off completely. Sweet almond oil softens the formula slightly. Rose fragrance oil scents the finished bar. Eight bars; hardens in 4-6 weeks.

items.prepNote: rendered beef tallow; 80% of oil weight; gives a very hard, white bar with fine, creamy lather
20% of oil weight; conditioning and a small lather boost
NaOH at 99% purity; calculated for 5% superfat
32% of oil weight; the lye solution liquid
3% of oil weight; added at light trace; rose fragrance oil holds better than rose EO through cure

content.text: Put on protective gloves and goggles. Pour the sodium hydroxide slowly into the distilled water in the HDPE pitcher, stirring until dissolved. The solution heats sharply to around 80°C and gives off fumes; do not lean over the pitcher. Cool to 38-42°C.
Melt the tallow gently, then combine with the sweet almond oil. Bring to 38-42°C.
Pour the lye solution into the fat in a thin stream. Stick-blend in 5-second bursts until the batter reaches light
Stir in the rose fragrance oil by hand. Pour into the mould, insulate, and leave 24-48 hours.
Unmould when firm. Cut into 8 bars wearing gloves. Cure on a ventilated rack for 4-6 weeks. The
is complete when a corner touched to the tongue gives no zap. Tallow bars get noticeably harder and whiter over the cure.
Store on a ventilated rack in a cool, dry place. Cured tallow bars keep 2 years. The rose fragrance is strongest in the first 6 months. The
from the sweet almond oil keeps the bar conditioning throughout. Discard at the first sign of orange spots (DOS) or a sharp, paint-like smell.
